definition: Supersede means to take the place of something older or less adequate.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word supersede. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know supersede should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The airline's new safety card supersedes the laminated one, though a few of the old sheets still lurk in seat pockets.
A patch is far milder than supersede — one fix stitched onto the old thing, which soldiers on, while a superseded rule is retired outright by whatever replaces it.
Update is milder than supersede: an updated edition is still the same living thing made current, while a superseded one is retired outright by its successor.

Displace means to push something out of its place or use — floods displace families, streaming displaced the video store — with no verdict on which thing is newer or better. Supersede adds order and legitimacy: the authorized newcomer takes over, and the old version is formally obsolete.

To succeed is to come after and take over in due course — the deputy succeeds the retiring chief, legitimately and on schedule. Supersede goes further: the newcomer does not merely follow the old one, it retires it, leaving the earlier version obsolete.

Until the 1950s, cargo crossed the oceans as 'break-bulk': sacks, barrels, and crates hoisted aboard one sling-load at a time by gangs of longshoremen.
Then Malcom McLean, a trucking magnate, began sending goods in sealed steel boxes of a single standard size, lifted from truck to ship by crane in under a minute.
Ports that adopted the container saw loading costs collapse, and within two decades the box had superseded break-bulk handling at nearly every major port in the world.
The change was not a gentle sharing of the docks.
Shipping lines rewrote their rules around the container, insurers priced the old methods out, and the sling and the cargo hook all but vanished from working ports.
A few museum piers still unload the old way for tourists — a reminder of a craft the standard box made obsolete.
